title: What happens when a university treats tuition fees as a strategic choice?
summary: The University of Buckingham has decided to reduce tuition fees on certain courses. Deba Bardhan Correia sets out the thinking behind the policy
full_text:
Towards the end of a recent conversation about the University of Buckingham’s decision to reduce tuition fees on selected undergraduate programmes, I found myself talking not about finance, recruitment or regulation, but about a seagull.

“Have you ever read Jonathan Livingston Seagull?” I asked. Jonathan is rejected by the rest of the flock because he refuses to fly simply to find food. Instead, he flies because he loves flying. The other seagulls cannot understand why he chooses a different path, but he continues anyway, finding fulfilment by refusing to conform.

“That’s how I see Buckingham,” I said. “We don’t have to fit into the rest of the flock.”

It is perhaps an unusual analogy for an article about tuition fees, but it captures something often missing from debates about higher education funding.

Buckingham’s decision to reduce fees by 45 per cent on selected courses generated headlines because universities rarely cut prices. But an equally interesting story lies behind the announcement.

Looking again at price

The decision did not emerge from a meeting looking for a headline as part of our 50th anniversary year. It began with conversations about price elasticity, market behaviour and changing student expectations, and shifting the dial from affordability to perceived value.

Students are comparing university not only with other universities but with apprenticeships, employment, and alternative pathways. They are weighing opportunity cost, debt and future earnings. Whether universities like that framing or not, they cannot ignore it.

Buckingham’s two-year degree model allows us to offer quality education with year-round access to academics at a reasonable cost. It already changes part of that calculation by enabling students to enter employment a year earlier and pay a year’s less accommodation costs in the summer.

However, conversations we have had with applicants suggested one financial barrier remained. Even if the long-term repayment picture is more nuanced under the student loan system – at Buckingham the standard UK tuition fee loan from Student Finance England does not cover the full cost of tuition, so our students contribute towards their fees while studying – prospective students focus first on the size of the commitment they are making today.

For us, we want to be at the forefront of the debate around the cost of higher education, and demonstrate the value of a two-year degree studied in a high-quality academic environment that focuses on knowledge, skills and high contact time with academics,

Testing the hypothesis

This is why we have launched a celebratory fees offer on selected courses that are showing growth in the market across business, humanities and social sciences, for intakes up to January 2028. For over half a century we have been innovating in the sector, and this initiative intends to tackle the subject of the cost of university by offering students the best possible quality and value for money in their study.

We want to continue to innovate and disrupt in the higher education market – it is in our DNA, having offered two-year degree programmes since 1976. As a smaller independent higher education provider that already specialises in accelerated degrees, we are in a unique position and possess the model to react to student demands around value for money.

We have listened to student feedback around the value for money offered by universities and want to demonstrate that there is a different approach. Now, we are taking the lead in the sector by reducing our fees; the nature of our two-year degrees means this initiative on applicable courses can lead to great savings with no compromise on quality. Practically, course content will remain the same, and student experience will not be affected by the fee reduction.

In our case, we have designed a model that uses our academic resources more intensively and efficiently across the year at a lower overall cost. The focus for us is not on matching a sector average – we want to demonstrate that it is possible to deliver a high-quality academic experience while providing better value for students.

Challenging inherited assumptions

None of this suggests every university should adopt the same approach. Different institutions have different missions, cost structures and student populations. A model that works for Buckingham may be entirely inappropriate elsewhere.

However, the sector should become more comfortable asking questions that would seem routine in almost any other industry. With the national debate centred on the affordability of higher education and the value of a degree, Buckingham is determined to lead in the debate and demonstrate that there is a different way to approach the challenge. In the face of issues such as advances in AI, high youth unemployment rates, and a volatile geopolitical environment, there is no one solution. The sector must change to meet the complex needs of the future.

That is why I return to Jonathan Livingston Seagull. The story is not really about flying; it is about having the confidence to think differently when others remain unconvinced. Universities routinely encourage students to question assumptions and challenge established thinking. As institutions, we should be prepared to do the same.

Buckingham’s fee initiative is most definitely not a declaration that we have solved the sector’s financial challenges. It is, though, a willingness to test a hypothesis rather than defend convention.

title: When the academic must become the evidence
summary: Rina Arya argues Jason Arday's death raises a wider question about the autobiographical burden placed on academics of colour who write about race
full_text:
Jason Arday died on 14 August, a week after resigning his professorship at Cambridge, with allegations against him still unresolved: plagiarism in his scholarship, and disputes over parts of the personal story in his memoir.

Whatever is eventually established, his family and friends are owed more than a case study; and we should be cautious about drawing firm conclusions from an unresolved case. But his death forces a wider question that should not be lost: why have racialised academics writing about race so often had to put their own biographies at the centre of their arguments, using their lives to show the damage that white privilege can do?

The unmarked norm

I know this territory because I have been there myself. In writing about race, cultural identity and institutional life, I have drawn on experiences that are mine, for good intellectual reasons.

Racism is structural but structures are not always visible; they become perceptible in encounters – in who is assumed to belong, who is interrupted, who is doubted, whose authority attaches effortlessly and whose must continually be demonstrated. Whiteness has long had the privilege of appearing not to be racial at all. It occupies the position of the unmarked norm. A white academic can enter a room without their presence being read through race. Telling one’s own story makes that asymmetry visible to people who have had the privilege of not seeing it.

There is a deeper problem with the neutral, disinterested voice of conventional scholarship prizes: it was never actually neutral but built from a particular vantage point and presented as though it belonged to no one. This is the central insight of standpoint theory. No perspective is entirely neutral, but some perspectives have historically been treated as if they were. Those who occupy the dominant position are rarely required to explain where they are speaking from, while those who name their own social position are more readily dismissed as subjective or partial.

Experiences can therefore be excluded from the scholarly record not because they matter less, but because they are not presented in a form that the discipline recognises as objective. First-person testimony can correct this. It is not a request for sympathy or an admission of victimhood, but an intellectual claim that an account of institutional life which omits how power is felt is incomplete.

The autobiographical burden

Here is the difficulty this creates. When this becomes an expectation – that racialised academics must disclose lived experience in order to establish that the power exists at all – we have what might be called “the autobiographical burden.” It is not enough to analyse racism. Academics of colour are asked to demonstrate it through themselves – the childhood incident, the moment of exclusion, the racist remark, the meeting in which authority evaporated, the occasion somebody mistook them for somebody more junior. The personal story can make concrete what a structural argument may otherwise leave abstract: the ways in which race continues to shape ordinary institutional life.

This burden falls not on racialised academics generally, but on those who write, or are invited to write, about race and cultural identity – a Black mathematician is rarely asked to establish their subject position before their findings are taken seriously.

Within that group, the asymmetry is stark. White academics writing about inequality are not required to excavate their biographies to establish their authority to speak, nor to catalogue the moments they benefited from whiteness before analysing white privilege; their relationship to the subject can stay intellectual. The racialised scholar is more often asked to make it personal – sometimes explicitly, by editors wanting the angle; sometimes self-imposed, because an abstract account of inequality is more easily contested, while a precise account of what happened to you is harder to wave away.

Once academics of colour use their own lives as part of the argument, questions about the argument can become entangled with questions about the person. Once the person becomes part of the evidence, their biography is also opened up to scrutiny. This is why the questions the Arday case raises reach beyond Arday himself, and why his death makes them more urgent, not less. Doubts about one scholar’s integrity or autobiography do not demonstrate the intellectual bankruptcy of lived experience, autoethnography or scholarship on race generally, and racial inequality does not reduce anybody’s obligation to tell the truth or properly attribute others’ work.

But nor should the truth of structural racism depend on the moral or biographical perfection of every person who describes experiencing it. We would not reject research on sexism because one feminist scholar behaved badly, or conclude class inequality had been disproved because a working-class commentator embellished their childhood. Racialised academics can still be made to stand for something larger than themselves – their success taken as evidence of racial progress, and their failings used to cast doubt on the structures they were trying to illuminate.

Making room to be ordinary

Universities have contributed to this.

Higher education has become adept at packaging individuals as narratives – the exceptional journey, adversity overcome, barriers broken, firsts achieved – celebrating diversity through people’s stories without confronting the harder business of examining how power operates within their own structures. Such stories humanise complex issues and inspire students, but they also turn racialised academics into symbols, and symbols are given very little room to be ordinary.

The risk is that a different expectation takes hold: that academics of colour should continually explain what race means through their own lives. We should be able to analyse race without making every relevant experience public, and to be afforded the same complexity and fallibility as anyone else – including the ordinary obligation to get one’s facts and citations right, which is a scholarly standard, not a racialised one.

None of this requires abandoning autoethnography, quite the opposite. First-person scholarship can reveal dimensions of institutional life that conventional evidence struggles to capture, making whiteness visible by describing what the apparently neutral institution looks like from a position it has historically failed to recognise as normative. Lived experience is a legitimate source of knowledge, but it should not become something that a racialised academic feels obliged to perform.

The Arday controversy should not lead to a retreat from first-person scholarship. That would be the wrong lesson. Autoethnography matters because it can reveal what more ostensibly detached forms of inquiry leave unseen. It also requires the same standards of truthfulness and attribution as any other scholarship. The challenge is to preserve the value of lived experience without allowing the credibility of a structural argument to rest too heavily on the biography of the person making it.

title: International students bring much more than money to the UK | Letters
summary:
Catriona McCarthy says enduring personal and professional connections should not be overlooked, while Graham Thompson says university leaders should shoulder some responsibility for their plight

The financial pressures described by university leaders (UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students, 14 August) are both clear and serious, yet there are wider consequences of declining international student numbers that deserve attention.

While the immediate economic contribution that international students make is significant, so is their broader value in bringing international perspectives to our campuses, enriching the learning experience, and strengthening the UK’s relationships, reputation and influence around the world.

full_text:
The financial pressures described by university leaders (UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students, 14 August) are both clear and serious, yet there are wider consequences of declining international student numbers that deserve attention.

While the immediate economic contribution that international students make is significant, so is their broader value in bringing international perspectives to our campuses, enriching the learning experience, and strengthening the UK’s relationships, reputation and influence around the world.

At a time when relationships, trust and influence increasingly matter, British Council research shows that studying in the UK can create enduring personal and professional connections. International graduates take those relationships into their careers, institutions and networks, maintaining connections with the UK long after their studies have ended, strengthening relationships, understanding and trust between the UK and countries around the world. UK universities are fundamental to that, and without them, this simply would not happen.

Catriona McCarthy

Interim director education, British Council

University leaders are right to warn of the financial turmoil in British higher education. Universities are undoubtedly facing uncertain futures. But those leaders must also shoulder some collective responsibility rather than reflexively laying blame elsewhere. It is a familiar refrain that when anything goes wrong the cause is external factors beyond the university’s control: first Covid, then energy prices and inflation, then frozen fees, and now the international visa system.

Any success, on the other hand, is claimed by university leaders as a sign of excellence. That excellence, however, is rarely managerial. Too many university leaders and senior managers have failed upwards from unexceptional academic careers to a gravy train of well-paid positions for which they lack the strategic foresight that would better serve their institutions.

This is the untold scandal of the higher education sector over the last decade. Did not one vice-chancellor understand that fees would not automatically increase with inflation after 2017 and put a plan in place to mitigate the effect on university finances? Did not the most basic analysis show that institutions were overreliant on international fee income?

title: The Guardian view on GCSE results: much to celebrate, much to reform | Editorial
summary:
Another post-pandemic cohort has shown its resilience and talent. But growing inequalities of outcome must be addressed

Most pupils who received their GCSE results this week were in the penultimate year of primary school when Covid struck, disrupting their preparation for secondary education. As with other post-pandemic cohorts, their achievements are therefore a testament to their ability, resilience and determination. A strong set of results, particularly in the core subjects of English and maths, should also be seen as a tribute to teachers dealing with ever expanding workloads.

Overall the impression is one of a welcome return to stability, as the legacy of the years of cancelled exams and teacher assessments is left behind. The proportion of top grades awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland rose compared with last year, but only by a tenth of a percentage point, while the overall pass rate fell by the same margin to 67.3% – the same as in 2019. Nevertheless, the latest results throw up familiar grounds for concern.

full_text:
Most pupils who received their GCSE results this week were in the penultimate year of primary school when Covid struck, disrupting their preparation for secondary education. As with other post-pandemic cohorts, their achievements are therefore a testament to their ability, resilience and determination. A strong set of results, particularly in the core subjects of English and maths, should also be seen as a tribute to teachers dealing with ever expanding workloads.

Overall the impression is one of a welcome return to stability, as the legacy of the years of cancelled exams and teacher assessments is left behind. The proportion of top grades awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland rose compared with last year, but only by a tenth of a percentage point, while the overall pass rate fell by the same margin to 67.3% – the same as in 2019. Nevertheless, the latest results throw up familiar grounds for concern.

The ongoing decline in language learning appears to be accelerating to an alarming degree, with GCSE take-up in French and other modern languages falling sharply again. A culturally enriching part of the curriculum is in danger of becoming the preserve of affluent state schools and the independent sector.

More broadly, inequalities of outcome suggest a fundamental change in approach is required to address regional disparities that have become entrenched. London schools once again pulled away from those in the north and the Midlands when it came to the awarding of top grades. Recent research has shown that good GCSE grades have a disproportionately beneficial impact on the life chances of pupils from less privileged backgrounds. A levelling up strategy is urgently needed.

While overall results in English and maths were impressive, a significant proportion of teenagers failed to achieve a grade 4 pass. The data also confirmed that the policy in England of imposing compulsory resits in those subjects is blighting lives rather than raising standards. Only 18.8% of those aged 17 and over achieved the requisite pass grade in English, down from last year, with an even smaller proportion achieving a grade 4 in maths. Far too many young people are becoming trapped in a demoralising and humiliating cycle of failure, which is blocking their progress into the world of work.

The government plans to introduce a new “stepping stone” qualification to build confidence ahead of resits, but a more radical overhaul is needed. At a time when an estimated 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training, developing a more nuanced approach, including alternative pathways, should be a priority.

An overhaul is what Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell, are promising. From 2028, the educational landscape in England may change significantly for 14- to 16-year-olds. The prime minister appears committed to rebalancing the curriculum by expanding the number of technical education options available to students, in a reprise of his approach as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

If a true parity of esteem is to be established between academic and vocational routes, as Mr Burnham desires, it will require a significant injection of resources. But the focus is the right one. Though there was much to celebrate as another post-Covid cohort came of age, the inequalities and failures revealed again by this year’s results are long overdue for attention.

title: International Applications Dropped 10% This Year
summary:
International Applications Dropped 10% This Year
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 08/20/2026 - 06:17 PM

Data from Common App shows increases from low-income student applicants, Black applicants and applicants from small towns.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
International student applications to American colleges dropped by 10 percent in the most recent application cycle—a decrease of roughly 16,000 students—according to data Common App released Thursday.

The figures show a major break from the upward trajectory of international applications over the past 10 years and reflect the impact of the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration policies. The landscape for international students in the United States has changed dramatically since the administration began revoking student visas, approving fewer new applications and limited the time international students can stay in the country. Department of Homeland Security data from the 2025–26 academic year showed an average 13 percent decrease in international student enrollment, and new projections say 112,000 fewer international students could be on U.S. campuses this fall.

The data represents applications to Common App’s 1,146 member institutions, which includes fewer than half of all public and private four-year colleges in the country.

Asia and Africa, which typically have the largest numbers of international student applications, saw the largest decreases—11 percent fewer applications from students in Asia and 17 percent fewer from students in Africa.

Rodney Hughes, a senior data scientist at Common App, said the decrease in international applicants is a significant departure from the way international student applications had been trending. International student applications had grown from about 90,000 to almost 165,000 a year between the 2016–17 and the 2024–25 application cycles. For the most recent cycle, the number of applicants dropped to 148,000.

“We have thought about what’s been going on over the past season and it’s interesting to differentiate the applicants, which is what we see here, from enrollments and just the thought process of applying,” Hughes said. “If you think, ‘OK, it might be hard for me to get a visa,’ that may make students more hesitant to apply.”

Despite the decrease in international students, Common App reported 1.5 million applicants in the 2025–26 application cycle—a year-over-year increase of about 2 percent. On average, each student applied to seven colleges, resulting in more than 10 million applications sent through Common App alone.

The modest increase in applicants comes as colleges around the country scramble to recruit and enroll a shrinking population of high school graduates.

Hughes said some domestic groups are growing faster than others. For example, the number of applicants who are low-income, Black or from small towns and rural areas is growing, even as the number of applicants from majority groups remains flat.

Common App doesn’t collect income information from applicants. Instead, it uses proxies to determine what percentage of students likely come from low-income backgrounds.

Since last year’s application cycle, 6 percent more students qualified for a fee waiver. And applications from students living in ZIP codes below the national median income level increased 8 percent, compared to a 2 percent increase in other applicants.

Meanwhile, Black applicants, who represent the third-largest racial group after white and Latinx applicants, are growing fastest. In 2025–26, the data shows an 8 percent increase in Black applicants, compared to a 2 percent increase in white applicants and a 3 percent increase in Latinx applicants.

The data also shows shifts in students’ geographies. Although nearly 90 percent of all applicants are from metropolitan areas, more than 25,000 students from small towns applied—a 9 percent increase. Meanwhile, about 17,000 students from rural areas applied, an increase of 8 percent.

title: Rethinking Calculus for Future Engineers
summary:
Rethinking Calculus for Future Engineers
Joshua.Bay Thu, 08/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

The University of Michigan is redesigning foundational math to connect calculus to real-world engineering—and get students to apply it earlier.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
For Siddhant Bohra, math had always felt relatively straightforward. But as he pursued robotics engineering at the University of Michigan, the 20-year-old found that the clean, theoretical problems he encountered in traditional calculus courses didn’t always resemble the challenges he wanted to tackle.

That changed last year when Bohra, then a sophomore, enrolled in ROB 201: Calculus for the Modern Engineer, a course that combines elements of Calculus I and II and differential equations with programming and robotics applications.

“I learn the best when I’m interested in something, and the only way I’m interested in something is knowing why or how this is going to help me,” Bohra said. “Sometimes you have to do things to learn, and not just read and figure out your interests from that. ROB 201 is that class that made me open my eyes to so many things.”

Redesigning calculus: First offered in 2024, ROB 201 was designed to more closely connect calculus with the work students would encounter as engineers, teaching them mathematics through computation, modeling and engineering projects.

Jessy Grizzle, a professor of robotics at the University of Michigan who developed the course, said the idea grew in part from years of hearing students describe a disconnect between the math they were learning and how they expected to use it as engineers.

“I kept hearing from students that they felt beat down in the math department and unmotivated by just learning abstract concepts without them being tied to applications,” Grizzle said. “People become engineers because they want to create devices that we all hope improve the world.”

“So when the math seems completely divorced from that, there’s a segment of students who are flat out turned off by that,” he added. “They really need it tied to something more substantial, more concrete.”

Grizzle structured the course around increasingly complex robotics problems. Rather than beginning with differentiation—as traditional calculus courses typically do—students start with integration, using real drone data to calculate a drone’s trajectory from its acceleration.

“I took the subject apart and rearranged it so that we started with integration, because it’s much easier than differentiation,” Grizzle said.

The course also pairs traditional pencil-and-paper calculus exercises that have exact solutions with messier, real-world problems students use computer programming to solve. Students learn to code in Julia, allowing them to use computation when a neat solution isn’t possible. Grizzle said the approach exposes students earlier to the kinds of challenges they will encounter as engineers, where data can be noisy and solutions less straightforward.

“We need to understand the hard [problems] because then we have confidence in how we can modify the procedure … [and] apply it in a more complicated situation that they’re facing on a student team, in an internship and eventually in a career,” Grizzle said. “We’re doing math with a purpose.”

ROB 201 isn’t the robotics program’s only departure from the traditional math sequence. In 2020, the program moved linear algebra, traditionally taken later in the math sequence, into students’ first year. Grizzle said the change gives students earlier exposure to mathematics foundational to robotics and machine learning while putting those who took calculus in high school and those who didn’t on more equal footing.

The change has also allowed students to reach a benchmark machine-learning course about a year earlier than those following the conventional math sequence, while performing similarly in the course, he said. The machine-learning course now enrolls about 300 students each year.

Refining the model: Student feedback also revealed a potential trade-off in ROB 201. Grizzle found that the course’s emphasis on coding and computational tools left some students with less practice performing calculations by hand, making them slower than their peers in subsequent engineering courses. Take-home assignments and readily available AI also made it easier for students to become overly dependent on computational tools.

As a result, Grizzle is adjusting the course this fall without abandoning the computational approach at its core. Students will take five low-stakes quizzes and an in-class final, which together will emphasize the hand calculations and foundational concepts they will need in later engineering courses. During those assessments, students can use limited handwritten notes, but not AI or software.

Homework and projects, meanwhile, will continue to emphasize coding and modern computational tools, allowing students to practice solving the kinds of complex problems they are likely to encounter as engineers. Grizzle said that includes teaching students how to use AI effectively rather than avoiding it altogether.

“Because AI is very important for a practicing engineer, I want them to learn how to do clean programming themselves,” Grizzle said. “And also how to get help from AI to do programming, and how to get help from AI as a tutor.”

Challenging the status quo: For Grizzle, being able to put what students learn in ROB 201 into practice is part of the goal. As part of a University of Michigan student project team, Bohra used concepts from ROB 201 to help program a navigation system for a mock Mars rover that competed in the international University Rover Challenge.

In ROB 201, Bohra worked on a project that used calculus to estimate and control the position of a drone. He said the experience became especially relevant when he later joined the rover team and encountered the same underlying mathematical concepts.

“When I was reading through the textbooks that my [project] lead gave me, all of the fundamental mathematics theory is what that ROB 201 project gave me,” Bohra said.

Bohra’s experience reflects what Grizzle sees as a larger question about how to define student success in a course like ROB 201. Passing calculus is one measure, but he also wants students to leave the course engaged, confident in their understanding of the fundamentals and prepared to apply them in later engineering courses.

Rethinking student success, Grizzle said, also means questioning long-standing assumptions about how calculus should be taught to engineering students.

“The course I created is much more helpful for most students, but the broader opinion of faculty across the College of Engineering is fear of changing from the old ways,” Grizzle said. “All faculty went through that sequence, even the faculty in engineering, and they’re afraid to move away from that because they’re afraid their students will be less prepared than they are.”

“Faculty want everything to be just like it was when they were students,” he added. “So we have a lot of work to do to get people to open their minds to the fact that novelty can be good.”

title: University suspends US academic leading Jason Arday plagiarism accusations
summary: Researcher Nathan Cofnas, an outspoken critic of DEI, was himself sacked from Cambridge in 2024 over his views on race.
full_text:
A Belgian university has suspended an American academic who led accusations of plagiarism against Jason Arday, the Black ex-Cambridge professor who died last week amid scrutiny many have labelled “racist“.

Arday had resigned from his post as professor of sociology at the University of Cambridge in early August over the scandal and the public scrutiny mounting against him.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items

list 1 of 4Cambridge professor Jason Arday quits amid plagiarism allegations

list 2 of 4UK PM Burnham reacts to death of former Cambridge professor

list 3 of 4Thousands mourn ex-Cambridge professor, blame ‘racist’ press for his death

list 4 of 4Jason Arday, former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism, found dead

end of list

Researcher Nathan Cofnas – a self-defined “race realist” who was himself sacked from his job at Cambridge in 2024 over his views on race – posted on X on Thursday: “I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me.”

Without naming Cofnas, the University of Ghent said in a statement that it had launched a “preliminary disciplinary investigation” against a postdoctoral researcher embroiled in the Arday case.

“Ghent University has suspended the staff member as a precautionary measure,” it said, citing its “respect for human dignity and opposition to discrimination”.

“We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial,” the university’s Rector Petra De Sutter and Vice-Rector Herwig Reynaert said in a statement. “However, that freedom is not unlimited. It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others.”

Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest-ever Black professor when he was appointed in 2023, was found dead on Friday aged 41. He was facing numerous accusations of plagiarising parts of his doctoral thesis and exaggerating some of his personal life achievements.

Diagnosed with autism and other developmental difficulties as a child, Arday had always disputed the allegations against him.

But Arday quit his job on August 5, writing in his resignation letter that he had “reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure”.

‘A case of institutional murder’

Plagiarism concerns surrounding Arday first surfaced several years ago, but went nowhere at the time, with one reporter backing down from investigating further after the professor threatened legal action.

Last month, however, Cofnas came forward to say he had found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor’s work – and the case snowballed, receiving widespread media coverage in the United Kingdom and the United States.

British media and right-wing commentators seized on the row, claiming Arday had unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

An outspoken critic of DEI, Cofnas argues intelligence differs between racial groups and wrote that in a true meritocracy, top universities like Harvard or Cambridge would hardly have Black professors.

“Arday’s harassment and death are not idiosyncrasies: they are very much a case of institutional murder by a system infused with anti-Black racism,” Oxford academic Sneha Krishnan wrote for Al Jazeera.

The former Cambridge University professor’s death led to anti-racist rallies in London and other cities, as tens of thousands mourned for Arday and blamed the media scrutiny piled on him.

Ghent University said it was now “assessing” whether there were sufficient grounds to launch full disciplinary proceedings in the case and that it is taking recent statements regarding this matter “very seriously”.

title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended
summary: An academic who made plagiarism allegations against Professor Jason Arday before his death has been suspended by a university.
full_text:
An academic who made plagiarism allegations against Professor Jason Arday before his death has been suspended by a university.

Prof Arday resigned from his role at the University of Cambridge this month after he faced intense scrutiny over accusations of plagiarism initially made by fellow academic Nathan Cofnas.

Mr Cofnas, who has advocated for "race realism", is currently a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University's department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.

In a post on X on Thursday, he said: "I am under investigation by my university for discriminating against Arday."

In a separate post, Mr Cofnas added: "I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me."

Ghent University confirmed his suspension after saying Prof Arday’s death "should prompt reflection", adding that the institution "opposes discrimination, hatred and racism".

The Belgian University said that while it supported academic freedom and open academic debate, "that freedom is not unlimited" and goes "hand in hand with responsibility" as it announced it was taking unspecified action regarding Mr Cofnas.

In a joint statement on yesterday, Ghent University rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert said: "Ghent University stands for respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism.

"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.

"It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others.

"For this reason, the university takes the recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously.

"Ghent University has decided to take appropriate action within its powers and the applicable framework."

The rector and vice-rector said that while it was "important to be transparent", they did not want to "pre-empt any potential decisions at this stage".

They said Ghent had been "shocked" by Prof Arday’s death and that their thoughts remain with his family, friends, colleagues and students.

A spokesperson for Ghent said in an update: "Ghent University formally notified the staff member concerned of the launch of a preliminary disciplinary investigation.

"As part of this process, the university is assessing whether there are sufficient grounds to refer the case to the competent disciplinary body for further consideration.

"Pending this preliminary investigation, Ghent University has suspended the staff member as a precautionary measure.

"The university cannot comment further on the specific details of the disciplinary case or the underlying arguments, in order to safeguard the confidentiality of the personnel file and the disciplinary proceedings."

Prof Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, was found dead in Battersea, south London, last Friday.

Earlier this week, organisers said more than 30,000 people had attended a vigil for the 41-year-old in Trafalgar Square, central London.

Speakers at the vigil criticised the press coverage of Prof Arday, with MP Diane Abbott saying he was subject of a "vicious" and "bitter" campaign by people who did not believe a black man should be a Cambridge professor – describing the press coverage of Prof Arday as a "public execution" and a "lynching".

Mr Cofnas has been contacted for comment.

title: Gen Alpha rises, one school at a time
summary: Inspired by Gen Z protests, students are now questioning their education leaders. Around 300 girls protested, forcing the administration to reconsider their school’s merger with a distant institution
full_text:
As the bell that signalled the end of the school day rang at 2.30 p.m. on August 18, scores of girls rushed out of Ujjain’s Maharani Lakshmibai Government Girls Senior Secondary School, Sarafa, with cheers and chants of victory. They were celebrating an assurance from the Madhya Pradesh government that their school would not be shut and merged with a school in Daudkhedi village, 6 km away. Many had tears in their eyes — they would be able to continue their studies.

Located opposite the famous Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga Temple in Ujjain, the government girls’ school was founded in 1959. Most students here come from the rural pockets around. The celebrations, teachers say, are a result of the girls’ struggle and courage that they showed as they raised their voices before government authorities.

On August 13, local newspapers had reported the merger of various schools. Under the Madhya Pradesh government’s ongoing merger exercise, 10 more schools, five each from Ujjain city and nearby villages, are being shifted to Daudkhedi, impacting 2,978 students, as per a March 30 order from the Department of Education. Sarafa was to be the 11th.

On August 14, a day before India’s 80th Independence Day, more than 300 girls of the school, most between Classes 9 and 12, gathered at the campus. Instead of going to their classrooms, they headed to the Ujjain Collector’s office and staged a protest against the government’s plans to shift their school.

The demonstration, videos of which went viral in no time, saw the girls, many with their parents, raising slogans against the move, even as some of them broke down. Two girls fainted. Finally, the administration assured them that their voices would be heard.

As per the government’s Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2023–24 data released by the Ministry of Statistics, India’s female literacy rate stands at 74.9% for those aged 7 and above.

Over the past month, school children in various parts of the country, mostly in India’s northern States ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), like Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Rajasthan, have risen up to question those in power. Protests are around the education system and its access: broken roads leading to schools, teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and toilets.

Gen Alpha rising

Most students were inspired by the Gen Z protests over question paper leaks and other irregularities in the competitive examination system. The protests had begun in New Delhi and then spread across the country, leading to the resignation of then Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, a move considered unprecedented for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Central government in its 12 years of rule.

The police brutality on students during their July 20 Sansad Chalo march to Parliament further angered a large section of the nation’s youth and their parents, a trusted voter base for the ruling BJP.

While the Gen Z protests largely involved college-going urban youth, the Gen Alpha uprising is seeing school students in small towns and rural regions questioning those responsible for their education. There is now a growing push for accountability and transparency.

On July 13, students of Eklavya Model Residential School (EMRS) in Chhindwara district’s forested Tamia tehsil raised angry slogans on the school campus alleging poor meal quality in hostels, saying there were worms in their food. Angry students, who gathered outside the school campus in the rain, demanded that the District Collector come and hear their woes. The school administration had not acted on their complaints, they said. The EMRSs are Union government-run institutions for students from tribal communities.

On August 15, a group of primary and middle school students from the Chandla area in Madhya Pradesh’s Chhatarpur district stopped the convoy of State Cabinet Minister and local MLA Dilip Ahirwar. They were angry about a broken road to their school, the absence of a boundary wall, and no electricity.

The same day, scores of schoolchildren, accompanied by some adults, from Chhatarpur’s Maharajpur tehsil set out on a 40-km march to the district headquarters over infrastructural woes, including a drain that swells in the rains, which the students have to cross to reach their school. Even though the march was stopped, as senior district officials went to meet the protesters, the protest went on for 18 hours and only ended after Maharajpur BJP MLA Kamakhya Pratap Singh met them after midnight.

On August 19, several children of a government primary school and their parents from Damoh district’s Arth Kheda village staged a demonstration at the Collector’s office over their school building. They said it was dilapidated and its roof could cave in with the rains. They raised slogans like, “Hum apna bhavishya maangte; hum apna school maangte (We demand our future; we demand our school).” They alleged that repair work in January did nothing for the building, and they were tired of administrative assurances. The school is currently being conducted at a temporary location in the village, a protestor said.

Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous State with over 200 million people, has so far witnessed four such demonstrations by Gen Alpha students in the last month in Hamirpur, Azamgarh, and Fatehpur, besides Lucknow, all over the lack of the basics.

On August 17 in Uttar Pradesh’s capital, Lucknow, over 200 students from Jai Prakash Narayan Sarvodaya Vidyalaya for Girls marched roughly 3 kilometres to the Dubagga-Kanpur bypass to protest against the shortage of teachers and inadequate basic amenities in their school. There have been similar protests in Rajasthan’s Alwar and Barmer districts and Bihar’s Gaya.

Governments feel the pressure

The August 14 protests by the girls in Ujjain prompted top BJP leaders and local officials to visit the school and hold discussions with the students on August 18, the next working day at the school, after the Independence Day-Nag Panchami weekend.

The protest held significance, as Ujjain is the hometown of Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav and a long-standing stronghold of the party that rules the State and is at the Centre. His sister, along with BJP MP from Ujjain Anil Firojiya and Ujjain North MLA Anil Jain Kaluheda, showed up at the school with several other administrative staff, including the District Collector.

“Chief Minister Mohan Yadav was informed about the proposal to relocate the Sarafa school to Daudkhedi. Keeping the convenience of the female students in mind, the Chief Minister immediately directed that their classes continue at the existing Sarafa school until alternative arrangements are made,” Firojiya said. He added that work would also be undertaken to construct a better school building after identifying a suitable site in the vicinity.

The quick outreach for the girls also holds significance, as women are considered a trusted voter base of the ruling BJP and were credited as an important factor in the party’s landslide victory in the 2023 Assembly elections despite anti-incumbency. After the meeting, a group of girls broke down while thanking the leaders.

Monika Sisodia, a Class 12 (commerce) student and one of the girls who led the protests, says, “While we were very disturbed when we found out that our school would be shifted, the August 13 news triggered us. We did not discuss our plans to protest with the teachers, but we decided to fight for our education.” Monika says that the girls had read about the Gen Z protests and were inspired by them.

“We have won the fight now, but we were ready to even go on a hunger strike to save our school. Had this not happened, many girls would have had to quit their studies,” says Monika, who dreams of becoming a police officer.

When asked if they feared online abuse, threats and trolling that many of the Gen Z protesters have had to face in the aftermath of their agitation, Monika and her peers said they are not active on social media.

A teacher, standing nearby, said, “Some of us teachers and parents were concerned about the possible consequences. So, we spoke to the students and advised them not to engage in any political slandering or language that may be problematic.” This came in the wake of criticism from a section on the Gen Z protests around abusive language.

Future and studies at risk

While the Sarafa school has got a lease of life, the 10 other schools to be merged with Daudkhedi are seeing dropouts. Prem Singh Parihar, who was the principal of Mahakal Maidan middle school, which has been merged, says that 117 students have taken their transfer certificates (TC) since April, bringing the school’s strength down from 282 to 165.

“Most parents who came to get the TCs had the same concern. They did not want to send their children so far. While some have borne the extra financial burden of sending their children to private schools nearby, there are a few who cannot afford it,” he says. More than 75 girls left the Sarafa school after their Class 10 results, with the news that their school would be merged, teachers at the school say. The overall strength of the school came down from 580 to 415 for the academic year 2026–27.

Nutan Middle School, Jaisinghpura, which has also been shifted to Daudkhedi, has seen 90 of its 300 students taking their TCs, as per data shared by the school. Ujjain Collector Singh, however, denies the dropout claims and says that some teachers who do not want to travel far to work are “making false claims” to prevent shifting.

The school in Daudkhedi has a modern building with 90 classrooms, facilities, and a large campus. The school is surrounded by fields and an open drain runs through its campus, making it unsafe.

Even though the government is currently running school buses for travel, students and parents have raised concerns for the children’s safety and the extra time spent commuting. For many students who travel from nearby villages, the distance to Daudkhedi goes up 15–20 kilometres.

Most of the students’ parents work as daily-wage labourers, while some drive autorickshaws or sell food and flowers in the temple town. They say that dropping and picking up their children from Daudkhedi will mean a loss of their daily earnings.

“My children leave at 7 in the morning by bus and return only by 7 in the evening. How will they study after a 12-hour day?” says the father of two primary school students, who now go to Daudkhedi. He works as a driver for a local BJP leader and does not wish to be named.

Many children also work after school to help their families financially and fear that extra travel time would hamper their work and studies alike.

Roshni Prajapati, a Class 11 (Arts) student at the Sarafa school, said, “My father drives an auto-rickshaw, so I make cotton lamp wicks after school and earn about ₹50 every day to help my family. There are many girls who sew or apply mehendi for some extra earnings. My parents, and many others, had told us that we may have to quit studies if our school was shifted.”

Several teachers and parents oppose school mergers but would rather not go public, fearing backlash from local BJP leaders and the administration in the future. “Officials have already asked school administrations to find out if the teachers had motivated the students to protest. Some of our names have already reached the authorities,” a senior teacher from a school says, requesting anonymity.

Burdened teachers and rising vacancies

On August 17, Vidhi Singh, 15, the daughter of a farm labourer and a student of Lucknow’s Sarvodaya Vidyalaya, walked over 2 kilometres in the rain. Her four companions suggested they take shelter until the rain slowed. She was resolute: “Let’s reach the bypass. Our march is more important.” Vidhi wanted to reach the spot where hundreds of others were protesting. “It may help to address the shortage of teachers,” she says. “Very few classes were being held due to the teacher shortage. This is impacting our studies in core subjects. We need qualified teachers immediately,” Vidhi adds. This year, she and her companions will take the Class 10 board exam.

In the heavy rainfall, the girls formed a human chain and sat down on the Dubagga-Kanpur bypass, demanding the Lucknow District Magistrate come to the site to address their concerns. They voiced their worries about the poor quality of food, the lack of medical services, power cuts, and high-handed staff. The demonstration followed an earlier demonstration on August 14, where over 100 students from the boys’ campus of the same institution, managed by the Social Welfare Department, blocked a road to voice similar concerns. Finally, senior officials from the Social Welfare Department and district administration engaged with the students, listened to their concerns, and escorted them back to the school. “We were promised that all our grievances would be solved within a week,” adds Vidhi.

Sadanand Mishra, a retired Government Primary School teacher in Lucknow, calls the protests the tip of the iceberg. He claims the crisis is much deeper and structural. “Most of the teachers’ working hours are spent on non-teaching duties like midday meal distribution, data collection, election duties, and HR processes like transfers and leave applications,” says Mishra, who is a member of the Uttar Pradesh Prathmik Shikshak Sangh, a teachers union.

A 2020 report by the National Institute of Educational Planning and Administration pointed out that only 19% of a teacher’s annual school-working hours were spent on teaching activities.

Mishra adds, “It’s been over five years with no job vacancy for primary teachers advertised in Uttar Pradesh. Numerous young people completing teacher-training degrees are waiting for job opportunities despite lakhs of posts vacant.”

A report published by NITI Aayog in November 2023 stated that there were 2.1 lakh vacant teaching positions across government schools in U.P.

On August 15, the Cockroach Janta Party, which was one of the entities that led the Gen Z protests, began its ‘School theek karo (fix the school)’ campaign. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke is visiting schools across the country and documenting the gaping holes in governance.

Days after the announcement and in the wake of Gen Alpha protests in some districts, the Rajasthan government imposed a restriction on outsiders entering government schools and barred photography and videography without written approval, while citing the “safety and privacy” of students. In an X post, Dipke asked, “All those working in the education department, including Ministers, officials, principals and teachers, should enrol their own children in govt schools. Then watch how quickly our govt schools magically improve. Why do all of them enrol their kids in private schools? Do they not trust their own work?”

title: IDP warns of further student volume drops as revenue plummets
summary:
IDP Education has based its FY27 outlook on market volumes being 20%-30% lower than in FY26, as tighter policy settings continue to affect global student mobility.

The post IDP warns of further student volume drops as revenue plummets appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The warning came as IDP – one of the three co-owners of IELTS – reported a 9% fall in revenue to AUD $795.4m for FY26.

Student placement numbers fell 27% during the year, while English language testing volumes fell 8%. Language teaching volumes increased 1%.

IDP said it earned more from each student and test than in previous years, helping to offset some of the decline in volumes.

“Our focus this year has been to manage financial performance whilst progressing the multi-year transformation program to reduce cost, simplify the business and position for future growth,” said IDP chief executive and managing director Tennealle O’Shannessy.

“The team has executed well in a dynamic operating environment with a focus on profitable revenue, and an ongoing commitment to quality and yield.”

The team has executed well in a dynamic operating environment with a focus on profitable revenue, and an ongoing commitment to quality and yield

Tennealle O’Shannessy, IDP

IDP cut around 1,250 roles, or 20% of its workforce, during the year. It also reduced its IELTS testing network from around 1,500 venues to fewer than 600.

The company said it reduced its costs by $32m during FY26, ahead of its $25m target. It plans to reduce costs by a further $15m in FY27.

Despite the fall in student numbers, IDP said it continued to see strong levels of trust among students. More than 90% of surveyed students said they trusted or highly trusted the company, while its student Net Promoter Score remained above 70.

The company is also investing in technology and AI-supported counselling, which it says is helping students find better matches with courses and universities.

O’Shannessy said the changing market could also create opportunities for IDP.

“Universities place increasing importance on student quality, compliance and enrolment certainty, and students rely more on trusted advice to navigate an increasingly complex international education landscape,” she said.

“IDP’s trusted role continues to grow.”

The company has also expanded its student placement offering into Malaysia and the UAE and opened 13 new IELTS centres in China.

“Our market-leading position, trusted brands, longstanding university partnerships and proprietary data position IDP strongly for the future,” she said.

“This positions us to deepen our relationships with students and university partners, capture more value across the student placement journey, and drive sustainable growth through a higher-quality, more resilient earnings profile.”

title: “They are not getting loans”: UK unis hits back at Reform’s claims on international students
summary:
UK universities have clarified claims by Reform UK that international students are claiming billions of pounds in student finance per year.

The post “They are not getting loans”: UK unis hits back at Reform’s claims on international students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
It follows a major policy from Reform UK that would bar “foreign students” from securing student loans at the same time as it launches a major push for apprenticeships. It claims that billions of pounds in savings could be put towards expanding apprenticeship programs for British businesses.

Reform UK education spokesperson and former UK home secretary Suella Braverman said: “We estimate that we can save about £2 billion from stopping foreign students from accessing student loans, which are taxpayer-funded.”

But UK universities have railed against the comments, clarifying that the vast majority of international students are not, in fact, eligible for UK student finance.

“International students are not eligible for UK student finance and they are not getting loans,” said Universities UK chief executive Vivienne Stern. “The students that Braverman is targeting are lawful residents who have settled status to live and work here permanently.”

The vast majority of international students are not able to get UK government funding for their studies – although may secure a student loan if they have indefinite leave to remain or hold EU settled status.

Irish students are also eligible for UK student loans. While HESA data shows that there more students from Ireland enrolled in UK universities than from any other EU country in 2024/25, this number sat at just 9,800.

The students that Braverman is targeting are lawful residents who have settled status to live and work here permanently

Vivienne Stern, Universities UK

Stern added that international students make a significant economic contribution to the UK to the tune of around £62 million per parliamentary constituency.

“Their fees ensure more opportunity for British students and support the innovative research that happens in towns and cities across the length and breadth of the country,” said Stern.

The government will introduce a levy on international student tuition fees at English universities in 2028, with the money this raises to be ringfenced and spent on maintenance loans for domestic students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Speaking at the press conference, Braverman went as far as to blast UK higher education. “We’ve got too many young people who are failing in our universities because they’re falling for the great university scam, signing up to £50,000 of student debt… for what? To study pointless subjects at mediocre universities,” she said.

But Stern hit back that a university education is still a positive choice for many students.

“For the majority of graduates, a degree pays off through higher average earnings, reduced likelihood of unemployment and a wider range of opportunities. Students should feel confident that their degree will set them up for a brighter future and equip them with skills they need to enter and succeed in the workforce,” she said.

“Universities already offer a great deal of vocational and technical education and are working closely with employers so students develop the skills our economy desperately needs, whatever they choose to study. Many graduates who did creative or specialist degrees go on to have highly rewarding and successful careers.”

title: Is the UK set up to flourish in a challenging international student recruitment market?
summary:
Viggo Stacey of QS analyses what’s next for UK international student recruitment as demand, competition and expectations shift.

The post Is the UK set up to flourish in a challenging international student recruitment market? appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
More prospective international students are expecting responses from institutions within 24 hours, demand Law, Medicine-allied subjects allied to Medicine and Creative Arts and Design on the rise while interest in Business and Management programs may have peaked.

These are the findings of Student mobility and motivation: UK, a new report by QS Quacquarelli Symonds. The big question is whether the UK is positioned to prosper in an evolving higher education market.

The unpredictability of the UK’s government, with six prime ministers since the Brexit referendum a decade ago and the instability of policy for higher education, has compiled the pressure on universities in the UK.

Universities UK pledged to ensure that the country’s universities serve the needs of the nation when Andy Burnham stepped into the role of Prime Minister earlier this summer.

But as Harry Anderson, UUKi’s deputy director (policy and global engagement), succinctly put it following the release of the new QS report, the research demonstrates the “enduring global appeal of UK higher education”.

But, he noted, that while the findings reinforce that the UK remains a destination of choice for students around the world, the “international student recruitment landscape is changing”.

“Universities are committed to delivering a world-class student experience, but at a time of increasing global competition, it is vital that the UK maintains a welcoming, stable and competitive environment for international students,” he said.

Vice-chancellors, university CFOs, teaching staff, students themselves, and increasingly policymakers and wider society, are aware of the financial pressures that UK universities are under.

The turmoil higher education is facing made the front page of The Guardian on August 14, while The PIE has diligently been keeping the international education sector up to date with the latest.

Changes to compliance and visa requirements in the UK have added an additional strain on international offices across UK universities.

The new QS research finds that the percentage of prospective students that expect responses from universities within 24 hours has risen to 27% in 2026 from 18% in 2022.

As the report sets out, UK universities have a significant opportunity in the evolving landscape, but policy volatility and the rise of lower-cost, high-quality alternatives in Europe, Asia and the Middle East are placing greater pressure on the UK’s competitive position.

“Sustained growth will depend on sharper market diversification, clearer employability messaging and a stronger articulation of value for students weighing cost, career outcomes and destination confidence,” it adds.

In the QS World University Rankings by Subject 2026, more than 170 entries from the UK placed in the top 10 globally in their respective subjects.

Higher education strategists may ask whether these outstanding programs are those being included in institutional messaging. Whether curricula and programming is shifting to align with demand. Whether the best UK university departments or courses are being included in TNE portfolios.

The UK’s universities continue to draw students through academic quality, global reputation and strong career outcomes. But as Andrew Plant, executive director for Europe at QS states, “The recruitment environment is shifting, with student choice becoming more complex, competition intensifying, and institutions under growing pressure to prove value earlier in the decision-making journey.”

“Growth will depend on how well institutions respond to changing source-market demand, affordability concerns, policy uncertainty and the rise of high-quality alternatives across Europe, Asia and the Middle East.”

The question is: is the UK ready to step up to the task?

title: The Evolution of Online Testing: Balancing Academic Integrity and User Accessibility
summary:
Image credit Unsplash

The way we learn in higher education has changed a lot, especially with the big move to online and hybrid classes. While virtual lectures and digital libraries are now standard, one area still sparks a lot of discussion: online testing. How can schools make sure students are playing fair when they're taking important exams from their own homes? This question has sparked a constant back-and-forth between keeping things secure and making sure everyone can access their tests. It's really made educators rethink what assessment even means.

From the Classroom to the Cloud: The Shift to Online Exams

Not long ago, proctored online exams were mostly for folks in fully remote degree programs. Most students would sit their midterms and finals in huge lecture halls, with a professor or TA keeping an eye on things. But then the pandemic hit, and suddenly everyone had to take their tests online. Schools rushed to find digital ways to replicate that controlled, in-person exam-room feeling. This urgent need led to the rapid adoption of tools and platforms designed to monitor students remotely. It kicked off a new era in academic testing, bringing unexpected challenges.

The Rise of Remote Proctoring and Its Challenges

To address cheating concerns, many universities began using remote proctoring software. These programs often use a student's webcam and microphone to monitor them during an exam. Sometimes, AI even flags "suspicious" stuff, like someone looking away from the screen or hearing background noise. Other tools lock down a student's browser so they can't hop to other websites. The idea is to level the playing field, but these technologies have raised serious concerns about privacy, fairness, and student stress. Students without a quiet, private space or reliable internet are immediately at a disadvantage.

This tension has created a kind of tech-driven cat-and-mouse game. As schools bring in stricter ways to proctor online assessments, some students feel cornered by what they see as invasive or flawed technology. They start looking for what they hope is the best and stealthiest bypass to feel like they have some control again. This reaction really shows a growing gap between what institutions want and what students actually experience.

The Student Perspective: Why Some Look for a Way Around

When students try to get around proctoring software, it's not always because they want to cheat. For many, it's about the intense pressure and anxiety that comes from being watched in their own personal space. That constant monitoring can feel like an invasion of privacy and can actually hurt the performance of students who already get nervous during tests. Plus, AI systems can sometimes flag students with disabilities or those who don't have a "standard" test-taking setup. This can lead to false accusations of cheating and a ton of stress. Feeling unfairly judged by an algorithm can erode trust and push students to find workarounds just to make their testing environment less stressful.

Innovations in Assessment: Moving Beyond Traditional Tests

Struggles with remote proctoring have led many creative educators to ask a different question: instead of building a better mousetrap, what if we changed the test itself? This has sparked new interest in other ways to assess students that focus on applying knowledge and critical thinking, rather than just memorizing facts. These kinds of tests are often naturally harder to cheat on. 

Think open-book exams where students have to put information together, project-based assignments that show skills over time, or portfolios that display a whole body of work. By designing assessments that measure learning in a more real-world way, educators can rely less on those high-stakes, heavily monitored exams.

The Role of AI in Maintaining Academic Integrity

Artificial intelligence is a mixed bag when we talk about academic honesty. While AI powers many of the proctoring tools that cause problems, it also brings new challenges with the rise of smart chatbots and text generators. This has forced a serious conversation on campuses everywhere. Many schools are now creating new rules and guidelines around academic integrity and teaching without AI, realizing that simply banning these tools isn't a long-term solution. The focus is shifting towards teaching students how to use these tools responsibly and designing assignments where AI help is either irrelevant or a documented part of the process.

Ultimately, how online testing changes isn't just a tech problem; it's about how we teach. Finding the right balance means more than just better software. It needs a commitment to building a culture of trust, embracing more genuine ways to assess learning, and using technology to help students learn, not just to police them.
